passage:
Interviewer: What did your family say?

I'm Vijay, and honestly it was Papa's one sentence: "We expected better." He wasn't shouting, and that was worse. I went up to the terrace and told myself I was the family's mistake. Then my sister Sarita came up with two cups of tea and said, "Papa is angry at what you did, not at you. Show him your plan." Next morning I sat down with Papa and Amma and a list. I said the true part first: I'd skipped classes and hidden my marks. Then the repair: I'd give Papa my attendance sheet every Friday and retake both papers in the summer. Papa read it twice and said, "Good. Now do it." It still stung. But it stopped feeling like being thrown out.

qa.q: What sentence from Papa left Vijay crushed?
What thought was crushing Vijay on the terrace, and what loosened it?
qa.a: Vijay believed that being "the family's mistake" was all Vijay was. Sarita's words that Papa was angry at the act and not at Vijay loosened that thought.
Taking a written plan to Papa and Amma worked because it admitted the true part, skipping classes and hiding marks, and offered a real repair with the Friday sheet and the summer retakes.

qa.q: How does Papa seem to see Vijay's list?
qa.a: Papa read it twice and said "Good. Now do it," so Papa seems to take it as a serious plan, while still expecting action rather than just words.

grounding: Shows family disappointment ('we expected better') heard as disappointment in an act, met with honesty and a repair plan, not proof of being unlovable.

passage:
Monday. Noor's father drove to the college in Bhopal after the principal called: Noor had been caught submitting a paid-for project. In the car Papa said only one thing. "We expected better from you." Noor stared at the dashboard, crushed. At home she locked her door and thought, they'll never love me the same way again.

Wednesday. Her brother Vijay knocked. "Papa isn't saying he doesn't love you. He's saying the thing you did was wrong. Those are different." Noor thought about that for a long time. The honest part was true: she had cheated. That part she could own.

Saturday. At breakfast, Noor said to her parents, "You're right, I did something wrong. I've asked the professor to let me redo the project on my own, and I'll accept the penalty." Papa put down his tea. "Good," he said. Then, after a moment, "Pass the jam, beta."

qa.q: What did Papa say in the car?
qa.a: Papa said, "We expected better from you."

qa.q: How did Noor feel after Papa's words, and what did she believe?
qa.a: Noor felt crushed and believed her parents would never love her the same way again.

qa.q: What helped Noor move from shame to repair?
qa.a: Vijay helped her see disappointment in an act is different from rejection, so she owned the cheating and shared a plan to redo the project.

qa.q: How might Papa see Noor's plan at breakfast?
qa.a: Papa seems relieved and proud of her honesty, saying "Good" and easing back into normal family warmth.

grounding: The three beats show a young woman crushed by her family's disappointment who hears the honest part, shares a repair plan and sees it is not rejection.

passage:
Aadhya, you think your parents will never forgive you for failing that semester? Let your Pradeep dada tell you what happened in 1970. I was twenty, studying in Allahabad, and I skipped classes for months to play cards. I lied in every letter home. When the results came, I had failed three subjects.

My father came on the train. He didn't shout. He said, "We expected better from you, Pradeep." That was worse than shouting. I felt like a stone had been put on my chest. I thought I had lost him.

That night I sat on the ghat for hours. Then I understood: he was disappointed in what I did, not finished with who I was.

In the morning I told him the truth about the cards and the lies. I showed him a timetable I'd written, for the re-exams. He read it, folded it into his pocket, and took me to eat kachori.

qa.q: How many subjects had young Pradeep failed?
How did young Pradeep feel when his father said "We expected better"?
qa.a: Young Pradeep felt crushed, as if a stone had been put on his chest, and feared he had lost his father's love.

qa.q: What turning point in the story led to repair?
qa.a: Pradeep realised his father was disappointed in the act, not in him, and then told the truth and showed a timetable for the re-exams.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's father have felt on the train to Allahabad?
qa.a: His father likely felt hurt and worried, but still cared, which is why he came in person and later took Pradeep to eat.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young man crushed by family disappointment who hears the honest part, shares a repair plan and learns it is not rejection.
